title: Dynamic Mirror context code versus fast-weight programmer
hypothesis: A shared slow controller can map live context to a compact functional coordinate that retrieves a task memory with fewer state bytes than explicit fast-weight updates, while generalizing to held-out context combinations.
physical_object: one shared linear slow controller and memory basis
logical_multiplicity: session/task memories selected by input context
controls: shared basis with static context IDs

development.allowed: validate held-out split, memory update rule, code fitting, payload bytes and interference

paid_objects: explicit fast weights or context code generator

success_gate: Held-out context query NRMSE <=0.05, no context leakage, and <=70% bytes of explicit fast updates; Mirror-specific claim requires beating generic context-to-code control.
failure_gate: Held-out NRMSE >0.20, static-ID-only control matches dynamic code, or generic MLP matches Mirror at similar bytes.
amendments: Development used a compositional rank-2 context rule; added a generic linear rank-2 control with the same function class as the Mirror code before fresh access. This prevents attributing a low-rank factorization benefit specifically to Mirror.
boundaries: Context combinations are held out by identity
